1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: The port served as a waystation for trade rather than a place where residents grew rich.
options.B: Amber from the north was the most valuable of the goods stored in the port's warehouses, outstripping ivory and glass.
options.C: The settlement was abandoned once the long-distance routes that stocked its warehouses shifted elsewhere.
options.D: The port's inhabitants kept their dwellings modest and uniform because their beliefs discouraged any display of wealth.

2.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Medieval masons lacked the knowledge needed to control how sound decayed inside a large stone building.
options.B: Evidence from building contracts indicates that cathedral reverberation was deliberately engineered rather than incidental.
options.C: Long reverberation follows inevitably from stone construction, whatever ceiling geometry a builder chooses.
options.D: Plainchant was sung slowly and without instruments in order to mask the acoustic flaws that stone interiors inevitably produce.

3.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to complete the text?

options.A: the highest gain recorded under Program A fell short of every gain recorded under Program B.
options.B: gains under Program B varied more widely across schools than gains under Program A did.
options.C: Program A's weakest school gained less than a tenth of what Program B's weakest school gained.
options.D: Program B's larger average gain rests on results from a quarter as many schools as Program A's does.

4.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.A: To demonstrate that Rapa Nui's forests were never in fact destroyed, contrary to the standard account.
options.B: To argue that the conventional 'ecological suicide' account misattributes a collapse that was largely precipitated by European contact.
options.C: To show that the islanders' own deforestation of Rapa Nui was the primary cause of a population collapse that came long before Europeans arrived.
options.D: To explain how rock-mulching gardens allowed islanders to keep farming deforested land and to sustain themselves there for centuries afterward.

5.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researcher's proposal?

options.A: The polish inside the batons' holes was produced by contact with wood rather than with hide or sinew.
options.B: The bored holes in batons recovered from one district match the diameters of spear shafts recovered from that same district.
options.C: Antler was harder to work with the available tools than the bone from which most other implements at these sites were made.
options.D: Batons with the most elaborate engraving show interior polish consistent with only brief use, while plainer batons show substantially heavier wear.

6.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.A: Octopuses rely on their colorblind eyes to coordinate the color changes that their chromatophores produce across the body.
options.B: Biologists were long puzzled by how an animal that cannot see color manages to match the hues of the surroundings it hides in.
options.C: Light-sensing proteins in an octopus's skin may explain how a colorblind animal matches its surroundings.
options.D: Chromatophores are pigment sacs ringed by muscles that expand or contract on command, spreading or concentrating the pigment.

7.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the passage's central claim?

options.A: Improved sanitation over the past century coincided with rising rates of allergy.
options.B: Children raised on farms with varied animal contact had lower allergy rates than urban children with comparable hygiene practices.
options.C: Exposure to a single common bacterium in infancy prevented most allergies.
options.D: Children in households that washed less frequently had lower allergy rates than other children, even when their contact with animals and older siblings was the same.

8.stem: Based on Text 2, which choice best describes how its author would evaluate the conclusion drawn in Text 1?

options.A: As irrelevant, because democratic legitimacy does not depend on the quality of decisions.
options.B: As mistaken, because voters are in fact well informed about most policy questions.
options.C: As correct, because individual voter ignorance necessarily invalidates democratic outcomes.
options.D: As too sweeping, since dispersed errors can offset one another under conditions Text 1 overlooks.

9.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence 'Foragers were not innocent of hierarchy; they policed it'?

options.A: It crystallizes the passage's central revision: that equality was actively maintained rather than merely given.
options.B: It concedes that foraging societies, for all their leveling techniques, were ultimately as hierarchical as the societies that followed them.
options.C: It restates the traditional claim that social hierarchy is natural and inevitable.
options.D: It introduces evidence that undermines the reliability of ethnographic methods.

10.stem: Which finding would most directly support the neuroscientist's proposal?

options.A: Birds deprived of sleep for a single night sang their practiced phrases with noticeably more errors the following day.
options.B: Sleeping birds showed neural firing sequences matching those recorded during daytime singing.
options.C: Birds that sang more phrases during the day spent more total time asleep.
options.D: Sleeping birds showed higher overall brain activity than birds that were awake.

11.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the historian's argument?

options.A: Coins from the period are concentrated in caches near fortified military camps along the kingdom's contested frontier.
options.B: The expansion in minting coincided exactly with the start of a major war.
options.C: The kingdom's total coin production remained constant throughout the period.
options.D: Coins from the expansion period are found distributed widely across market towns far from any garrison.

12.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

options.A: It presents a longstanding interpretation, grants the conditions that made it plausible, and then overturns it by reinterpreting the same evidence.
options.B: It weighs two competing schools of modern criticism against each other over how the marks in the fascicles should be read.
options.C: It argues that the dashes must be preserved in print precisely because Dickinson never prepared the poems and her intentions can never be recovered.
options.D: It traces how editors who once regularized the dashes gradually came to appreciate their deliberate artistry.

13.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.A: contains a systematic error of about forty minutes introduced in the course of copying.
options.B: rests on observations gathered over a longer span of time than the northern table's.
options.C: records observation at its own house rather than transmission of the northern figures.
options.D: was copied from the northern table and afterward corrected by a later reader.

14.stem: Which finding would most strengthen the passage's proposed explanation of why the correlation weakened?

options.A: Children whose past promised rewards had frequently failed to appear waited less, whatever their measured self-control.
options.B: Children who waited longer for the promised second treat went on to score higher on achievement tests administered decades later.
options.C: Training in later childhood can measurably improve a child's self-control.
options.D: Adjusting for the children's measured intelligence sharply reduced the tie between waiting and later achievement.

15.stem: On which of the following points would the authors of the two texts most likely disagree?

options.A: Whether waste and corruption occur in the administration of aid
options.B: Whether aid's life-saving benefits are worth its effect on the development of accountable institutions
options.C: Whether inexpensive health interventions save large numbers of lives
options.D: Whether governments that receive substantial aid come to depend on donor funding rather than on taxes raised from their own citizens

16.stem: Which choice best states an inference supported by the text?

options.A: The lizards' shuttling behavior is driven primarily by external temperature rather than by time of day.
options.B: On overcast days the lizards must generate more of their own body heat internally, since basking on exposed rock is unavailable to them.
options.C: Deprived of direct sun for a full day, the lizards cannot hold the body temperature they require and do not survive the night.
options.D: The shade of vegetation offers the lizards no thermal benefit at all once the sky has been overcast for the whole day.

17.stem: Which choice best states what Oduya's year-long tracking implies about meadow grazing?

options.A: Dominant tortoises drove smaller rivals from the island's meadows, which is why only the largest individuals fed there.
options.B: Competition among tortoises had no measurable effect on any aspect of how they fed or moved.
options.C: A tortoise's access to meadows depended on its own physical development rather than on displacing competitors.
options.D: Smaller tortoises kept to the forest edge because its cover offered richer forage than the open meadows.

18.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to complete the text?

options.A: the single-stream scheme collected about 4.5 kilograms more per household each week than the sorted scheme collected.
options.B: the material rejected under the single-stream scheme came to about as much as the total collected under the sorted scheme.
options.C: the sorted scheme's rejection rate was roughly a tenth of the single-stream scheme's, and its households set out roughly half as much material.
options.D: each scheme delivered about 6.6 kilograms of uncontaminated material per household per week.

19.stem: Which finding, if true, would most support the researcher's demand for evidence of a genuine causal effect?

options.A: Residents who already exercise regularly are more likely than their neighbors to seek out homes in the districts where parks are plentiful and well maintained.
options.B: Across dozens of cities, park density and residents' reported health are strongly and consistently correlated.
options.C: After a new park opened, chronic-illness rates fell among nearby residents relative to comparable residents in similar neighborhoods that got no park.
options.D: The neighborhoods with the most parkland also report the highest average household incomes anywhere in the city.

20.stem: Which observation would most support the mechanism described in the text?

options.A: As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.
options.B: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
options.C: Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years, shedding meltwater from its margins at rates that tracked each summer's temperatures.
options.D: Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.

21.stem: Which result would most directly support the psychologist's hypothesis?

options.A: Participants allowed to finish every puzzle recalled them better than participants interrupted partway through.
options.B: Participants recalled the puzzles they never completed more accurately than those they finished.
options.C: Participants recalled all of the interrupted puzzles equally well, whether or not they later finished them.
options.D: Participants reported enjoying the puzzles they completed more than the ones left unfinished.

22.stem: Which choice is best supported by the study described in the passage?

options.A: Departure timing had no measurable effect on the birds' winter survival.
options.B: Late-departing birds arrived at their wintering sites much later than birds that left on time.
options.C: Birds that made frequent stops during migration arrived in worse condition than those that did not.
options.D: Late-departing birds compensated for lost time in ways that left them weaker and less likely to survive.

23.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the recent model's claim?

options.A: Central and peripheral chambers experience nearly identical rates of predation.
options.B: Subordinate birds on the periphery gain measurable warmth from the collective mass of the nest during cold desert nights.
options.C: Peripheral birds that attempt to move toward the central chambers are aggressively driven back by dominant pairs.
options.D: Colonies with more residents fledge more chicks overall than smaller colonies do.

24.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the chant's reputation for antiquity (its 'authorizing fiction')

options.A: proves that the chant contained no genuinely old musical material.
options.B: accurately reflected the melodies' unbroken transmission from the early Church.
options.C: lent the standardized liturgy a legitimacy its recent origins might otherwise have lacked.
options.D: was deliberately fabricated by singers who knew the chant to be new.
